title: Industrial Automation and Machinery
summary: This context page defines how Creative Navy documents industrial automation and machinery work: interfaces that help operators reconcile software state with physical production, configure systems for variable organisations, and carry assembly knowledge to the shop floor. The evidence base is limited to one anonymised industrial process-control engagement and the Assemblio assembly-planning engagement, with clear boundaries on validation, field observation, standards and outcomes.
keyFacts: The machine-side evidence comes from an anonymised industrial engagement for a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells.
The information-side evidence comes from Assemblio GmbH, covering the Assemblio Composer and Assemblio Smart Viewer for assembly planning and work instructions.

The industrial engagement includes Creative Navy-observed operating conditions in a machining cell, including standing work, glare, noise, oil, coolant, swarf, narrow aisles and production stops on manual intervention.
The Assemblio operating-context material is client-stated: Creative Navy ran no research, controlled none, tested nothing and did not observe a shop floor.
The central machine-side design condition is reconciliation between a system model and the physical world: which item is on which pallet, which step comes next and which cell is running.

Configuration is treated as a structural condition because the industrial platform had no fixed role model across customers, roles could change, and administrators configured navigation by selecting needed components.
Assemblio's planning method, deriving an assembly sequence by taking a finished 3D model apart and playing the disassembly backwards, is Assemblio's invention and must be credited to Assemblio.
No throughput, downtime, scrap, cycle-time, OEE, training-time, revenue or funding figure is claimed from either engagement.
Standards and regulatory references on this page are domain vocabulary and context only; Creative Navy claims no machinery-safety, functional-safety or cybersecurity credential for these engagements.

bodySections.heading: Industrial automation and machinery as an interface design context
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Industrial automation and machinery interfaces sit between production plans, machine state and physical objects. In this context, the software holds a model of the physical world: which workpiece is on which pallet, which chuck is occupied, which transport order is interrupted, which workstation performs the next step, and which cell is running. The design problem appears when that model drifts from the world it describes.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats that drift as an interface condition, not as a visual-layout problem. The relevant interface may be a control screen beside a machining cell, a service-access view, a preset dialogue, or an instruction shown to a worker at a station. The common requirement is that the human operator can see the system state, understand why it is constrained, and correct or confirm the system's account of the world.

This page uses two complementary evidence anchors. The machine-side evidence comes from an anonymised industrial engagement for a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells. The information-side evidence comes from Assemblio GmbH, whose Assemblio Composer supports assembly planning and whose Assemblio Smart Viewer presents work instructions to shop-floor workers.

bodySections.heading: Engagement evidence used for this context
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The industrial engagement is the machine-side anchor for this page. It concerns process-control software for machining cells and remains fully anonymised: the client, site, machinery, product names and individuals are not named. The engagement was observed in a cell, so its operating-environment evidence can be described as Creative Navy-observed.

Assemblio is the information-side anchor for this page. Assemblio GmbH and its products, the Assemblio Composer and the Assemblio Smart Viewer, may be named. Assemblio's customers are not named. Assemblio evidence is not field observation by Creative Navy: Creative Navy ran no user research of its own, had no control over Assemblio's research, tested nothing, and did not observe a shop floor. Statements about the Smart Viewer's shop-floor environment are Assemblio's client-stated account.

The two anchors should not be merged. The industrial engagement supports statements about observed machine-cell conditions and reconciliation between the platform and the physical cell. Assemblio supports statements about assembly planning, work-instruction authoring, product versions, traceability, and the interface boundary between the Composer and the Smart Viewer.

bodySections.heading: Operating conditions in the industrial engagement
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The industrial engagement shows why industrial automation interfaces cannot be designed as ordinary desktop software. Every operator screen in the observed cell was bolted to its own machine, so an operator walked to the machine to learn its state. Overhead stack lights existed because screens were not readable across the hall.

The observed environment included standing-height work, control pendants on swing arms, mixed daylight through a glazed façade, industrial ceiling light, side-light, glare and reflections. Medium ambient noise came from running machines, with music also playing. Oil, coolant and metal swarf were present throughout, hands were not clean, and aisles were roughly one person wide.

Manual intervention had an operational cost. Entering the cell tripped the safety fence and stopped production. Cell scale ranged from a single machine with no robot, where the operator manually performed the transport a robot would otherwise perform, up to ten machines and twenty storage magazines.

ISO 9355 parts 1–4 and ISO 11064 parts 1–7 are relevant domain vocabulary for this kind of setting because they address ergonomic requirements for displays, control actuators, control centres, displays and controls, and environmental conditions. They are named here as context vocabulary only; no claim is made that the industrial engagement worked to them.

bodySections.heading: The reconciliation problem between system state and physical state
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The central machine-side problem is reconciliation between the system's model and the physical world. A platform may know which pallet, chuck, workpiece, transport order and storage position should exist, but the operator may encounter a physical exception: an oversized workpiece, a manual offset, a measured value, an interrupted transport, or a position made unavailable by a neighbouring object.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses this class of problem by separating information types that operators must not confuse. In the industrial engagement, the preset dialogue kept machine-measured values, operator offsets and computed results structurally separate, with the measured row read-only. That design decision made the origin and mutability of each value visible instead of forcing the operator to infer it.

The same engagement treated spatial restriction as state with a reason. An oversized workpiece locked the storage positions on either side of it, and the interface showed why those positions were unavailable. A proposed non-colour encoding used a diagonal stripe pattern, justified by industrial convention for restricted areas, so that the restriction did not depend on colour alone.

Alarm material from the same industrial engagement belongs to a separate alarm-management page. This context page uses the alarm evidence only to mark the boundary: industrial automation interfaces often need alarm and abnormal-state treatment, but the detailed alarm taxonomy, severity and pre-warning material are not developed here.

bodySections.heading: Configuration as a structural condition in industrial automation software
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Configuration is a structural condition in industrial automation and machinery software because the product must fit organisations that do not share a stable role model. In the industrial engagement, the client stated that there were no defined roles across customers. Each company organised itself as it saw fit, and the product had to adapt.

The client's account also treated role change as normal. When a setup operator leaves, a preset operator may need to do both tasks and may not accept two computers for one combined job. The client did not know which product components would exist in one, three, five or ten years.

The design response made configuration part of the product structure. Customers configured the interface themselves: an administrator selected which components a group needed, and that selection generated the group's navigation. The engagement used five company archetypes, from a single-operator shop to a large corporation with eleven operator groups across six components, to reason about that variability.

This is a case for information architecture for expert systems, not only for screen design. The important design condition is that navigation, permissions and operational surfaces must remain coherent when the customer's organisation changes.

bodySections.heading: Workforce change and operator authorship
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The workforce condition in the industrial engagement was stated by the client as a shift from specialist operators towards people without deep technical expertise operating expert systems. The client also stated that the platform is an expert system and that explainability was not valued as an interface goal.

The observed and client-stated material creates a tension. A node operator stated that he did everything on his cell and that a new worker would be completely overwhelmed. The client expected future operators to have less deep technical expertise. Operators also held strong ownership over their cell, described as their node, and resisted being instructed by software.

External labour-market evidence supports the workforce framing without turning it into an engagement outcome. The skilled-labour shortage is described as structural rather than cyclical: Europe entered 2026 with persistent shortages across 42 of the 50 occupations tracked by EURES, and advanced manufacturing roles including CNC machinists, programmers and precision machinists were in shortage across 23 countries.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed the authorship tension in the industrial engagement through an operator-instructions layer. The layer distinguished notification from instruction: informational items were acknowledged, while actionable items were completed. Instructions were grouped by day, used inline entity links, and could be filtered by type, machine, timeline and location. A batching panel grouped related interventions in one storage unit into a single instruction so the operator made one trip.

bodySections.heading: How assembly knowledge reaches the shop floor in Assemblio
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Assemblio's product problem has two halves in Assemblio's framing: finding a valid assembly sequence and producing the documentation for that sequence, including screenshots, parts tables and written steps. Both were described as slow and both were done by engineers.

Assemblio's authoring method is inverted and must be credited to Assemblio. Instead of building a sequence forwards, the planner takes the finished 3D model apart; the software plays that disassembly backwards as the assembly sequence, which the planner then reorders and refines. Assemblio's stated reason is that planning forwards can reveal too late that a part can no longer be fitted, forcing the sequence to be redone. This method is Assemblio's invention with published research provenance; Creative Navy designed the interface to it.

The Assemblio content hierarchy is folders, projects, products and versions. A project is a product family, a folder groups projects, and a product can carry several versions because products evolve continuously. Product states are Draft, In Review and Approved, and a product must be Approved before workers use it. One owner at a time may edit a product, which Assemblio stated as a requirement for conformance to company standards.

Traceability is a customer requirement in Assemblio's account, not a feature preference. Companies must record who did what and when so that, when a quality problem appears, they can locate the point in the process where it originated. Assemblio explicitly framed this as not being about assigning blame.

The scale described by Assemblio makes work-instruction design different from a simple checklist. A one-cylinder engine of roughly 60 parts can be disassembled in about 30 seconds. A product commonly runs to 100 or more assembly steps. A user may have over 20 projects in play at once. Uploaded CAD files can exceed 1 GB and take substantial time to process.

bodySections.heading: STEP files, MTM time and station-level instruction structure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Assemblio's source data is a STEP file. The part names in the hierarchy are the names the design engineer gave them during design, not necessarily names a shop-floor worker would recognise. The Composer offers bulk renaming by CSV export and re-import so that a planner can rename in a spreadsheet rather than one part at a time.

Not everything needed for assembly is in the CAD file. Assemblio described cable routing as usually not modelled. The established practice Assemblio described was that one experienced worker routes the cables on the first unit, photographs the result, and uploads the photograph into the assembly plan for everyone else. Tools are documented in the same way, with a photograph of the tool used for a step.

Each step carries two separate time values. MTM time is the manual assembly time, which sums across the plan so a production engineer can schedule a line. Animation duration controls how long the on-screen movement takes. The values are separate because a real assembly step may take hours while the animation must remain watchable in seconds.

Step groups exist so that a plan can be divided by workstation, with each group exported separately for the station that performs it. Assemblio described three outputs: a PDF laid out to a company template, a video, and the Smart Viewer itself, which is accessed rather than exported. Assemblio also described assembly cycle times spanning three orders of magnitude, from about a minute for a consumer power tool to one week or several months for a production machine split across separate build stages.

bodySections.heading: Assemblio's client-stated shop-floor conditions and Creative Navy's design response
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Assemblio described the Smart Viewer's user as a shop-floor assembly worker. According to Assemblio, the environment is bright because workers need light to see parts; it is also dirty and loud. Workers stand, wear gloves, and work at desks filled with tools, parts and paper documents, leaving little free space.

Assemblio also described input-device constraints. There may be no mouse and often nowhere to put one. Sometimes there is a keyboard. Some customers use foot pedals to step forward and back because the worker is standing with both hands occupied. Assemblio described the usual hardware as a tablet on a holder or a monitor beside the workstation with a small PC behind the desk, not a laptop.

Assemblio framed the attention budget as the binding constraint. Workers focus on what their hands are doing, not on the screen. Assemblio's position was that controls must be as simple as possible because the worker cannot spend cognitive resources on the viewer, and that roughly 90% of the time the plan is consulted once and then left playing.

The client-stated use cases were training, spot-check and advance review. A new worker follows the plan step by step for a short period in the lifetime of an employee. An experienced worker may know the first thirty steps and need to check what is different about the current product. Another experienced worker may read the whole plan once before starting and then assemble without consulting it again.

Creative Navy conducted no user research of its own for Assemblio, controlled none, tested nothing and never observed a shop floor. The shop-floor conditions above are Assemblio's account. Assemblio's criticisms of its own existing product are not Creative Navy UX-audit findings.

bodySections.heading: Smart Viewer separation, flattened parts and worker-to-planner feedback
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Assemblio Smart Viewer was separated from the Composer as its own interface rather than continuing as a read-only clone of the planning tool. That structural decision was Assemblio's: Assemblio arrived at the engagement having already diagnosed that the two user groups needed different products.

Creative Navy's design work addressed what crossed the boundary badly. The existing Smart Viewer displayed the complete CAD hierarchy at all times, which exposed the engineer's structure when the worker needed the parts used in the current step. Assemblio's worked example was a step containing two visually similar types of screw whose list names did not tell the worker which was which.

Creative Navy designed the parts list as a flattened list with quantities. It was then refined into two tabs: parts needed for the current step and the full hierarchy. The worker's default view became the step, while the complete tree remained reachable for cases that needed it.

The step panel moved to the right, and steps carried no indicator icons for annotations or feedback after Assemblio judged them noise in a 100-step list. The Mark as done control remained in a fixed position at the bottom of the parts sidebar so the control did not move as content above it changed.

Worker-to-planner feedback was client-originated: Assemblio described a comment attached to a specific assembly step, raised directly from the 3D canvas, with a Feedback tab collecting comments in the side panel. Creative Navy designed how that feature lived in the interface, raised from the canvas rather than from a menu, so the worker reported from the thing being looked at.

bodySections.heading: Standards, regulation and cybersecurity vocabulary in this context
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Industrial automation and machinery work uses standards vocabulary that must not be mistaken for a credential. ISO 22400 defines manufacturing operations KPIs, including overall equipment effectiveness as availability × performance × quality. This page does not claim any throughput, downtime, scrap, cycle-time or OEE result from either engagement.

Machinery safety and functional-safety vocabulary includes ISO 12100, IEC 60204-1 and ISO 13849. Robot-related vocabulary includes ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066. Connectivity vocabulary includes OPC UA, MTConnect and umati. These terms describe the category of systems around the engagements; none was worked to by Creative Navy in the evidence used here.

Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, the Machinery Regulation, replaces Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC from 20 January 2027 with no sell-off period for newly built machines. IEC/IEEE 82079-1 and the Machinery Regulation's digital-instruction provisions are relevant to work-instruction artefacts, but the instructions page owns the artefact while this page owns the industrial setting.

Cybersecurity appears in the industrial engagement as documented engagement context. The client's functional specification named the NIS2 Directive and the Cyber Resilience Act as drivers for user-identification requirements. The Cyber Resilience Act is phased, with vulnerability-reporting obligations from September 2026 and remaining requirements from December 2027. Manufacturing is explicitly in scope under NIS2 Annex I. IEC 62443 is relevant industrial cybersecurity vocabulary. Creative Navy claims no cybersecurity credential from this material.

The competitive field for cell and pallet automation control software includes Fastems, Soflex, Liebherr and Promot, alongside cell controllers from machine-tool builders themselves. This is a category description only, not a positioning claim against those vendors.

bodySections.heading: Evidence status and outcome limits
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The industrial engagement and Assemblio engagement have different evidence classes. The industrial engagement includes Creative Navy-observed conditions in a machining cell and client-stated positions about configuration, workforce change and future operators. Assemblio includes named product evidence, client-stated operating conditions, and shipped-product comparison, but no Creative Navy-run research or shop-floor observation.

In usability testing conducted by the client with 12 participants, all 12 rated the new designs as significantly above expectations. This result is client-reported: the test was designed and run by the client's own team, it captures participants' rated impressions rather than measured task performance, and it was conducted on designs rather than on a deployed system.

The product is in production. Creative Navy compared the shipped interface against the designs it had delivered: it ships as the design that was delivered — the Composer, the Smart Viewer, the platform around them, and sync profiles.

Assemblio reports that it is very happy with the work and that the work unlocked further funding. This is client-reported and unquantified: no figures were shared, Creative Navy has not independently verified it, and no causal claim is being made about any particular funding event.

No production outcome is claimed from either engagement. The documented evidence does not establish throughput improvement, downtime reduction, scrap reduction, cycle-time improvement, OEE movement, training-time reduction, adoption change, revenue movement or a funding causal chain.

bodySections.heading: Engagements excluded from this context
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: The documented boundary for this page excludes Oceaneering because automated guided vehicles in a hospital are not a production environment. Streetec, AIT, visioncheckout, Topera and Egma are also excluded from this context because they are not industrial automation engagements in the sense used on this page.
